summary: Maps the Policy Core Information Model to a form implementable in a directory accessed through LDAP. It defines structural classes for policy data and relationship classes showing how they connect, plus some classes added only to speed up retrieval of large amounts of policy data. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Policy rules are written in a common blueprint language. This turns the blueprint into forms that can be stored in a directory, so network tools can save and fetch the rules.

questions: how to store network policy in ldap
what is the policy core ldap schema
subtitle: How network policy rules from the Policy Core Information Model are stored in an LDAP directory.

tldr.problem: The Policy Core Information Model describes policy rules in a way that is independent of storage, but implementations that keep policy in an LDAP directory need concrete object classes and attributes.
tldr.mechanism: The Policy Core LDAP Schema (PCLS) maps the model's classes to LDAP classes and attributes, turns its associations into DN references or tree containment, and adds extra classes that let a client fetch lots of policy in few requests.
tldr.outcome: Implementations that keep policy in an LDAP directory and follow RFC 3060 SHALL use this schema or a schema that subclasses it. RFC 4104 updates it.

today: RFC 3703 is a Proposed Standard that is updated by RFC 4104. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Scope and Starting Point
sections.content:
RFC 3703 starts from the object-oriented information model for policy in RFC 3060 (the Policy Core Information Model, PCIM) and maps it to a directory accessed with LDAP. Here, policy means a set of rules to administer, manage and control access to network resources. The RFC notes this is not the meaning of "policy" in X.501.

The schema uses the prefix pcim and contains 23 classes in all. Structural classes of the model map nearly one-for-one to LDAP classes, and model properties map to LDAP attributes. Relationship classes are mapped in three ways: to auxiliary classes, to attributes holding distinguished names (DNs), and to superior-subordinate containment in the directory tree.

Implementations that use an LDAP directory as the policy repository and want to implement policy information according to RFC 3060 SHALL use this schema or one that subclasses it. RFC 3060 is a prerequisite, because the detailed meaning of the classes appears only there.
sections.eli5: There is a plan for how to describe network rules. This document shows how to file those rules in a big shared cabinet that computers can search.

sections.title: Mapping Classes and Associations
sections.content:
Class names start with a lowercase letter in LDAP, because X.500 does not allow class names that begin with an uppercase character. PolicyGroup, PolicyRule and PolicyRepository each become three LDAP classes: an abstract one, an auxiliary subclass that can be attached to another entry, and a structural subclass for a standalone entry. This gives the directory designer maximum flexibility.

Associations in the model become DN-reference attributes or tree containment. For example, PolicyGroupInPolicyGroup maps to pcimGroupsAuxContainedSet and PolicyRuleInPolicyGroup maps to pcimRulesAuxContainedSet. Conditions and actions of a rule use tree containment or the lists pcimRuleConditionList and pcimRuleActionList.

The RFC removed DIT structure rules and content rules from the schema because many LDAP servers support them unevenly and they would need OIDs. It instead describes where such rules could be used. Entries can be named with a class-specific name attribute, with cn, or with orderedCimKeys, and the RFC recommends against combining them into a multi-part RDN.
sections.eli5: Each kind of thing in the plan gets a matching form in the cabinet. Things that point to each other get little notes saying where the other one is filed.

sections.title: Rule-Specific and Reusable Conditions and Actions
sections.content:
The model separates conditions and actions that belong to one rule from reusable ones that several rules can share. A rule-specific condition or action is normally removed with its rule, usually has the same access permissions as the rule, and needs fewer directory accesses. A reusable one must have permissions expressible without a rule, and needs a separate access each, but only has to be updated once when many rules use it.

The schema expresses the difference with auxiliary classes and tree placement. Conditions and actions are auxiliary subclasses of pcimConditionAuxClass and pcimActionAuxClass, and all such subclasses MUST be auxiliary. For a rule-specific case they attach to an association entry under the rule. For a reusable case they attach to an entry under a repository, and the association entry holds a DN reference to it.

A rule can also carry its conditions and actions directly. Such a simple policy rule is limited: all conditions are ANDed together and actions have no order. A complex rule uses separate entries, and is needed for other condition combinations or ordered actions.
sections.eli5: Some instructions belong to just one rule, like a note stuck to it. Others are on a shared card that many rules can point to, so you only fix the card once.

sections.title: The Policy Rule Classes and Attributes
sections.content:
The abstract pcimRule class represents the "If Condition then Action" meaning of a policy rule. Its subclasses are pcimRuleAuxClass (auxiliary) and pcimRuleInstance (structural). Attributes include pcimRuleName, pcimRuleEnabled, pcimRuleConditionListType, pcimRulePriority, pcimRuleMandatory, pcimRuleSequencedActions and pcimRoles.

Values are checked against their allowed ranges. For most invalid values, the RFC says the policy rule SHOULD be treated as disabled. A pcimRulePriority of 0 means "don't care", and a larger number is a higher priority.

Per-condition details live in pcimRuleConditionAssociation, which has a group number for the DNF or CNF expression and a negation flag. Action ordering lives in pcimRuleActionAssociation through pcimActionOrder: smaller positive values come earlier and zero means order does not matter.
sections.eli5: A rule is like a sign that says: if this is true, do that. It also has settings such as whether it is turned on and how important it is.

sections.title: Time Validity Periods
sections.content:
The auxiliary class pcimTPCAuxClass lets a rule be enabled or disabled on a schedule. It is named this way because the full name from the model, pcimTimePeriodConditionAuxClass, is too long for some directories. A rule is scheduled active if it is active according to at least one of the time period entries it references through pcimRuleValidityPeriodList.

The attributes include pcimTPCTime (a start and end separated by a slash, where the start can be THISANDPRIOR and the end THISANDFUTURE), a 12-bit month mask, a 62-bit day-of-month mask, a 7-bit day-of-week mask and a time-of-day range. pcimTPCLocalOrUtcTime is 1 for local time and 2 for UTC, and UTC is assumed if it is absent.

Values that do not match their format SHOULD be treated as errors and the rule disabled. The RFC warns against subclassing this class to add domain-specific properties such as IPsec or QoS; those belong in separate condition subclasses combined with validity periods.
sections.eli5: A rule can have a calendar that says when it counts, like a school bell that only rings on weekdays.

sections.title: Finding Policy Efficiently
sections.content:
A Policy Decision Point (PDP) must find the policy entries that apply to the devices it serves, without making too many LDAP requests. The schema provides a toolkit rather than one required layout. The key class is pcimSubtreesPtrAuxClass, whose multi-valued attribute holds DNs of subtrees that contain policy objects.

The PDP is configured with one starting DN, reads the pointers on that entry, then asks each referenced subtree for entries whose object class is pcimPolicy. For servers that cannot match auxiliary classes, entries can instead be tagged with the keyword POLICY in pcimKeywords. The class pcimElementAuxClass tags entries from outside the policy classes, for example an address range, so they are found too.

In the best case, in the RFC's example, a PDP needs exactly three LDAP requests. A PDP SHOULD understand these optimizations but MUST still work, less efficiently, without them.
sections.eli5: Instead of opening every drawer, the computer reads one note that says which drawers hold the rules, then goes straight to those.

sections.title: Extending the Schema
sections.content:
For standardized schemata, domain-specific information MUST be put in auxiliary subclasses of pcimConditionAuxClass and pcimActionAuxClass. Making them structural would lose the choice between rule-specific and reusable use. Non-standardized schemata are RECOMMENDED to do the same.

For vendor-specific content there are pcimConditionVendorAuxClass and pcimActionVendorAuxClass. Their data attributes hold octet strings, and a separate attribute holds an OID that says how to read them. These are for vendor extensions, and standardized extensions SHOULD NOT use them. The RFC's example is one policy server managing devices from several vendors.
sections.eli5: If you need a new kind of rule, you add a new sticker to the cabinet instead of rebuilding it. Special company-only stickers come with a label that says how to read them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The PCLS is not directly usable in a real system without the discipline-specific mappings, such as DiffServ or IPsec, that other documents define. Those documents must add their own security considerations. Specific security requirements MUST be defined for each operational real-world application of PCIM.

Some policy values may stand for scarce or costly resources and must not be disclosed or changed by unauthorized parties. General LDAP security considerations from RFC 3377 apply. The RFC points to RFC 2829 (authentication methods) and RFC 2830 (TLS extension) as the tools for authentication and authorization of directory access.
sections.eli5: The cabinet by itself does not lock anything. Whoever sets up a real system has to decide who may read or change each rule and add locks.
